title: The Psychology of Money, lesson 1 - no one is crazy

slides.head: 5 Reasons Smart People Make _“Crazy”_ Money Choices
slides.note:
from The Psychology of Money
by Morgan Housel

slides.head: You've judged someone's money choices.
body: Too careful. Too reckless. Lottery tickets. Panic selling.
From the outside it looks crazy. *Morgan Housel says it probably isn't.*

terms.def: The tiny slice of history you've lived through. It quietly writes most of what you believe about money.
Every money decision makes *sense to the person making it*, given what they've lived through.

slides.title: You've only lived a tiny slice of money history
slides.what: Money has a history stretching across centuries and continents. Each of us has lived through *only a sliver* of it, yet that sliver shapes most of what we believe.
slides.try: Ask: _“Which of my money beliefs did I simply inherit from my timing?”_

slides.title: Your birth year can write your money beliefs
slides.what: Born in 1950? US stocks went almost nowhere in your teens and twenties, after inflation. Born in 1970? They grew *almost 10 times* over the same stage of life.
slides.try: Ask: _“What did the markets do when I was 20?”_

diagram.note: US stocks after inflation, teens to twenties

slides.title: Your early years set your appetite for risk
slides.what: Economists Ulrike Malmendier and Stefan Nagel studied decades of data. People's willingness to take risk tracked *what the economy did in their own lifetimes*, especially their early adult years.
slides.try: Ask: _“Am I cautious because of facts, or because of what I saw at 25?”_

slides.title: Reading about a crash isn't living through one
slides.what: You can study a market crash in a book. But living through one, with your job and savings on the line, teaches a lesson that *sticks far longer* than any chart.
slides.try: Before taking money advice, ask: _“Has this person lived through what they're describing?”_

slides.title: “Irrational” choices often make sense up close
slides.what: Lower-income US households tend to spend more on lottery tickets than wealthier ones. From outside it looks irrational. But with no other visible path, a ticket *buys a dream* that feels within reach.
slides.try: Swap _“Why would anyone do that?”_ for _“What would make that feel sensible?”_

slides.head: Before you judge a money choice, ask two questions
steps: _“What years and experiences taught them this lesson?”_
Then ask the same question *about yourself*.
Go easy on everyone: index funds and retirement accounts are only a few decades old. We're all still beginners.
slides.challenge: Which of your money beliefs came from the years you grew up in?

slides.head: Which one changed how you see _money_?
slides.body: Save this, and send it to the friend whose money choices you never understood.
